triage.name: Emphysema
triage.reason: Chronic progressive dyspnea with clear risk factors, exam findings and spirometry; overlaps with COPD and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, good teaching case.

auto-repaired: workup: 'CT chest without contrast (high-resolution)' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Severe disease, atypical presentation, or evaluation for lung-volume-reduction surgery)

auto-repaired: workup: 'Alpha-1 antitrypsin level' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Emphysema before age 45, lower-lobe predominance on CT, or family history of AAT deficiency)
auto-repaired: workup: 'ECG' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if Signs of right heart strain or palpitations)
exam: term 'Accessory muscle usage' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Most common in current or former smokers
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema at an earlier age

risk_factors.text: Occupational exposure to dusts, fumes, or chemicals

family_history: COPD or emphysema in a first-degree relative
social_history: Workplace exposures to dusts or fumes

chief_complaints.text: I get short of breath when I walk
I cough up mucus every day

hpi.duration: Months to years before presentation; daily symptoms by the time of diagnosis
hpi.progression: Dyspnea on exertion slowly worsens over years; cough and sputum become more frequent; later dyspnea occurs at rest
hpi.quality: Breathlessness with chest tightness and wheezing
hpi.severity: Progresses from mild exertional limitation to severe dyspnea with minimal activity
hpi.timing: Worse with exertion; may be constant in advanced disease

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling in the ankles or legs

atypical.how_it_differs: Many older adults attribute gradual dyspnea to aging or deconditioning and present later, often with fatigue, reduced activity, or an acute exacerbation rather than a chief complaint of breathlessness.
missing_classic_features: Clear report of dyspnea on exertion

atypical.how_it_differs: Obesity can make dyspnea on exertion easier to attribute to weight and may delay recognition; lung exam may be less impressive, and sleep-disordered breathing often coexists.

general.mild: Appears comfortable at rest; no visible respiratory distress during the interview
general.moderate: Comfortable at rest but becomes short of breath when walking across the room; may purse lips during expiration
general.severe: Dyspneic at rest, leaning forward with shoulders braced; accessory muscle use and difficulty finishing sentences
general.critical: Severe respiratory distress, cyanotic or pale, tripod position, unable to speak in full sentences

findings.maneuver: Inspect the chest and compare the anteroposterior diameter with the lateral diameter
Observe breathing at rest and during conversation
Observe the neck and shoulders during quiet breathing
findings.finding: Visible use of accessory muscles of respiration

findings.maneuver: Observe the chest during quiet inspiration
findings.finding: Inward movement of intercostal spaces during inspiration

findings.maneuver: Auscultate and time the expiratory phase
Percuss the chest in all zones
Inspect the lips and nail beds

findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Inspect the fingers and nail beds

labs.caveat: Chronic hypercapnia occurs with advanced airflow obstruction and hypoventilation; a normal PaCO₂ does not exclude emphysema.
Hypoxemia worsens as ventilation-perfusion mismatch progresses; often normal in mild disease.
Secondary polycythemia can develop from chronic hypoxemia; many patients instead have anemia of chronic disease.

findings.finding: Tall, peaked P waves in inferior leads (P pulmonale)
Low QRS voltage in limb leads
Poor R wave progression in precordial leads
Right ventricular hypertrophy pattern (tall R in V1, deep S in V6)

findings.text: Increased retrosternal airspace on lateral view

imaging.preferred_when: Assessing severity, bullae, atypical distribution, or surgical evaluation

findings.text: Centrilobular emphysema, predominantly in upper lobes
Panlobular emphysema, predominantly in lower lobes (more common in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency)

initial.why: Evaluates hyperinflation, bullae, and alternative causes of dyspnea
Screens for anemia or secondary polycythemia

confirmatory.why: Demonstrates persistent airflow obstruction: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC < 0.70; confirms COPD/emphysema pattern

supporting.why: Assesses gas exchange and chronic hypercapnia
supporting.only_if: SpO2 < 92%, severe airflow obstruction, or suspected cor pulmonale

supporting.why: Characterizes emphysema distribution and bullae; used for surgical or transplant evaluation
supporting.only_if: Severe disease, atypical presentation, or evaluation for lung-volume-reduction surgery

supporting.why: Detects alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in patients with early-onset or lower-lobe-predominant emphysema
supporting.only_if: Emphysema before age 45, lower-lobe predominance on CT, or family history of AAT deficiency

supporting.why: Evaluates for cor pulmonale and arrhythmias
supporting.only_if: Signs of right heart strain or palpitations

not_indicated.why: No role unless pulmonary embolism is suspected
Not helpful for diagnosing emphysema; elevated only with left heart failure or severe cor pulmonale

decision_points: Spirometry with bronchodilator is essential to confirm airflow obstruction; do not rely on symptoms or imaging alone.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing should be considered in patients with early-onset emphysema, lower-lobe predominance, or a family history.
Arterial blood gas should be obtained when chronic hypoxemia or hypercapnia is suspected (SpO2 < 92%, severe disease, or cor pulmonale).
CT chest is reserved for surgical planning or atypical presentations; it is not needed for routine diagnosis of emphysema.

criteria.name: COPD diagnosis (GOLD criteria)
criteria.summary: Persistent airflow limitation on post-bronchodilator spirometry (FEV1/FVC < 0.70) in a patient with compatible symptoms and exposure history. Emphysema is confirmed by imaging or pathology showing alveolar destruction.

differential.name: Chronic bronchitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic productive cough and exertional dyspnea in a current or former smoker

history: Prominent daily productive cough for at least three months per year for two years
Less complaint of chest tightness or hyperinflation
exam: Wheezing and coarse breath sounds without marked barrel chest
labs: Spirometry shows obstruction, but the clinical picture is cough-predominant
imaging: Chest X-ray may show increased bronchovascular markings rather than hyperlucent, hyperinflated lungs

differential.name: Asthma
differential.why_considered: Episodic dyspnea, wheezing, and cough that may improve with bronchodilators

history: Onset often in childhood or early adulthood
Symptoms vary with triggers such as allergens, cold air, or exercise
No significant smoking history in many patients
Symptoms may be absent between attacks
exam: Wheezing predominantly expiratory, but lung exam may be normal between exacerbations
No barrel chest or marked hyperinflation when stable
labs: Spirometry typically shows reversible airflow obstruction, with significant FEV1 improvement after bronchodilator
imaging: Chest X-ray usually normal, or hyperinflation only during severe exacerbations

differential.name: Congestive heart failure
differential.why_considered: Exertional dyspnea with edema or orthopnea, especially in an older patient
differential.trigger: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, bilateral crackles, or elevated jugular venous pressure

history: Known coronary artery disease, hypertension, or prior myocardial infarction
labs: Spirometry may show restriction rather than obstruction
imaging: Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, prominent pulmonary vasculature, or interstitial edema
Echocardiogram shows systolic or diastolic dysfunction

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: Acute or worsening dyspnea, especially with pleuritic chest pain or risk factors
differential.trigger: Sudden-onset dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, or risk factors such as recent surgery, immobility, or cancer

history: Acute onset of dyspnea or chest pain
Risk factors: recent surgery, immobilization, active cancer, previous venous thromboembolism
Often no chronic progressive exertional limitation
exam: Clear lungs or only focal crackles
labs: ABG may show hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis
Elevated BNP or troponin in right heart strain
imaging: CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defect in pulmonary artery

differential.name: Pneumothorax
differential.why_considered: Sudden dyspnea and unilateral chest pain in a patient with emphysema or bullae
differential.trigger: Acute unilateral pleuritic pain with sharply worse dyspnea and asymmetric breath sounds

history: Sudden sharp chest pain, often pleuritic
History of large bullae or prior pneumothorax
May occur after coughing or without trauma
exam: Decreased or absent breath sounds on one side
labs: Usually not helpful; ABG may show acute hypoxemia
imaging: Chest X-ray shows visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripherally
Tension pneumothorax shows mediastinal shift away from the pneumothorax

differential.name: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
differential.why_considered: Emphysema at an early age, lower lobe predominance, or family history of COPD
differential.trigger: Emphysema before age 45, no or minimal smoking history, or lower lobe emphysema on CT

history: Family history of emphysema or liver disease
May have unexplained chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis
exam: Similar findings to usual emphysema, but may present at younger age
No specific exam feature differentiates from smoking-related emphysema
labs: Genetic testing confirms ZZ, SZ, or other deficiency genotypes
imaging: CT shows panlobular emphysema, predominantly in lower lobes

severity.mild: Mild exertional dyspnea with heavy activity; no symptoms at rest. Spirometry shows obstruction but FEV1 is generally ≥80% predicted. Imaging may demonstrate hyperinflation.
severity.moderate: Dyspnea with moderate activity such as walking on level ground at a normal pace. Exam shows prolonged expiration, decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance. FEV1 is typically 50–79% predicted, and resting SpO2 is usually normal.
severity.severe: Dyspnea at rest or with minimal activity. Accessory muscle use, pursed-lip breathing, hypoxemia, and often chronic hypercapnia. FEV1 is typically 30–49% predicted. Patient may be cachectic and have signs of cor pulmonale.
severity.critical: Acute or chronic respiratory failure with severe hypoxemia and/or worsening hypercapnia. Altered mental status, cyanosis, inability to speak in sentences, and hemodynamic instability can occur. Requires immediate ventilatory support or intensive care.

red_flags.finding: Acute onset of pleuritic chest pain with unilateral absent breath sounds
Sudden worsening dyspnea with hypotension or tachycardia
red_flags.meaning: Pulmonary embolism or tension pneumothorax; emergency imaging needed

red_flags.finding: Altered mental status or somnolence with rising PaCO2
red_flags.meaning: Hypercapnic respiratory failure; prepare for ventilatory support

red_flags.finding: Fever, increased sputum purulence, and new infiltrate
red_flags.meaning: Acute exacerbation due to respiratory infection; may require antibiotics and hospitalization

red_flags.finding: Inability to speak full sentences, accessory muscle use, SpO2 <88%
red_flags.meaning: Impending respiratory failure; escalate care immediately

red_flags.finding: Peripheral edema, elevated JVP, loud P2

special_populations.differences: Present later, often with fatigue or deconditioning; dyspnea may be attributed to aging. Exacerbations are more frequent and severe; polypharmacy and comorbidities complicate management.

Restrictive physiology may mask hyperinflation on exam and imaging; sleep-disordered breathing often coexists and worsens hypercapnia. Weight loss can improve dyspnea but may exacerbate muscle wasting.

key_questions.question: How long have you been short of breath, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic progressive exertional dyspnea over months to years, not sudden onset

key_questions.question: What activities make you short of breath, and how far can you walk before stopping?
key_questions.looking_for: Quantified exertional limitation, e.g. dyspnea after walking one flight or a short distance

key_questions.question: Do you have a cough? Do you bring up phlegm? What is it like?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic productive cough, usually worse in the morning, without hemoptysis

key_questions.question: Do you ever hear wheezing or feel tightness in your chest?
Have you smoked cigarettes, or do you currently smoke? How many packs per day for how many years?
What kind of work have you done? Any exposure to dust, chemicals, or fumes?
key_questions.looking_for: Occupational or environmental exposures that can cause emphysema

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had emphysema, COPD, or liver disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history suggesting alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you had frequent chest infections, like bronchitis or pneumonia?
Have you lost weight without trying?
Any swelling in your ankles, feet, or legs?
Have you had any sudden sharp chest pain or sudden worsening of shortness of breath?
Have you coughed up blood?
key_questions.looking_for: Hemoptysis suggests another cause such as cancer or bronchiectasis

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever, chills, or a change in your phlegm color or amount recently?
Which inhalers, nebulizers, or oxygen do you use, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Current bronchodilator/corticosteroid use and response; chronic oxygen therapy

key_questions.question: Have you had the flu or pneumonia vaccine?

reasoning_points: Older adult with a long smoking history presenting with chronic progressive exertional dyspnea
Chronic productive cough, wheezing, and chest tightness
Exam shows hyperinflation with barrel chest, decreased breath sounds, prolonged expiration, and hyperresonance
Spirometry demonstrates persistent airflow obstruction: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70
Chest imaging shows hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, and increased retrosternal airspace, with possible bullae
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency considered if early onset, lower-lobe predominance, or family history
Differential diagnosis includes chronic bronchitis, asthma, congestive heart failure, pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax
Absence of fever, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, and acute onset helps exclude infection and acute vascular events

easy: Older current or former smoker with classic barrel chest and exertional dyspnea
Spirometry shows fixed obstruction with FEV1/FVC <0.70
Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms
medium: Patient with chronic bronchitis overlap: cough-predominant picture
Woman with fewer pack-years or secondhand smoke exposure
Mild disease where exam findings are subtle and spirometry is borderline
Patient with coexisting obesity masking hyperinflation
hard: Young patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and lower-lobe emphysema
Minimal smoking history but significant occupational exposure
Patient presenting with pneumothorax as first manifestation of emphysema
Concurrent congestive heart failure with crackles and edema making diagnosis unclear
